questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a new system of units, the units of mass, length, time and current are $5$ kg, $5$ m, $5$ s and $5$ A, respectively. If $\mu_0$ and $\epsilon_0$ are the permeability and permittivity of free space, respectively, then in this new system of units, the magnitude of one SI unit of $\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}$, is:
questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for permeability of free space $\mu_0$ is $[M L T^{-2} A^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for permittivity of free space $\epsilon_0$ is $[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 A^2]$.

The dimensional formula for $\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_0}{\epsilon_0}}$ is:
$\left( \dfrac{[M L T^{-2} A^{-2}]}{[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 A^2]} \right)^{1/2} = \left( [M^2 L^4 T^{-6} A^{-4}] \right)^{1/2} = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$

Let the magnitude of $1$ SI unit in the new system be $n$. Using the principle of dimensional homogeneity:
$n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2$
$1 \times [M_1 L_1^2 T_1^{-3} A_1^{-2}] = n \times [M_2 L_2^2 T_2^{-3} A_2^{-2}]$

Given the new units are $M_2 = 5$ kg, $L_2 = 5$ m, $T_2 = 5$ s, and $A_2 = 5$ A, while the SI units are $M_1 = 1$ kg, $L_1 = 1$ m, $T_1 = 1$ s, and $A_1 = 1$ A.

$n = \left( \dfrac{M_1}{M_2} \right) \left( \dfrac{L_1}{L_2} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{T_1}{T_2} \right)^{-3} \left( \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} \right)^{-2}$

$n = \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)^{-3} \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)^{-2}$

$n = 5^{-1} \times 5^{-2} \times 5^3 \times 5^2$

$n = 5^{-1 - 2 + 3 + 2} = 5^2 = 25$

Thus, the magnitude of one SI unit in the new system of units is $25$.

Answer: $25$

questions.q: A temperature difference can generate e.m.f. in some materials. Let $S$ be the e.m.f. produced per unit temperature difference between the ends of a wire, $\sigma$ the electrical conductivity and $\kappa$ the thermal conductivity of the material of the wire. Taking $M, L, T, I$ and $K$ as dimensions of mass, length, time, current and temperature, respectively, the dimensional formula of the quantity $Z=\frac{S^2 \sigma}{\kappa}$ is :-
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{S}=\text{ emf per unit temperature difference } \\ & \sigma=\text{ Electrical conductivity } \\ & \mathrm{k}=\text{ Thermal conductivity } \\ & {[\mathrm{S}]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{I}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]} \\ & {[\sigma]=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^{-3} \mathrm{~T}^3 \mathrm{I}^2\right]} \\ & {[\mathrm{K}]=\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^1 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]} \\ & {[\mathrm{Z}]=\frac{\mathrm{S}^2 \sigma}{\mathrm{~K}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^1 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~K}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^1 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]}}\end{aligned}$
$[\mathrm{Z}]=\left[\mathrm{K}^{-1}\right]$

questions.q: A dimensionless quantity is constructed in terms of electronic charge $e$, permittivity of free space $\varepsilon_0$, Planck's constant $h$ and speed of light $c$. If the dimensionless quantity is written as $e^\alpha \varepsilon_0^\beta h^\gamma c^\delta$ and $n$ is a non-zero integer, then $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta)$ is given by
questions.solution:
For the quantity to be dimensionless
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{e}^\alpha \varepsilon_0^\beta \mathrm{h}^\gamma \mathrm{c}^{\mathrm{d}}=\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0 \mathrm{~A}^0 \\ & \Rightarrow(\mathrm{AT})^\alpha\left(\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^{-3} \mathrm{~T}^4 \mathrm{~A}^2\right)^\beta\left(\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right)^\gamma\left(\mathrm{LT}^{-1}\right)^\delta=\mathrm{A}^0 \mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0 \\ & \therefore \alpha+2 \beta=0, \alpha+4 \beta-\gamma-\delta=0,-\beta+\gamma=0 ~\&~-3 \beta+2 \gamma+\delta=0 \\ & \therefore \alpha=-2 \beta, \beta=\gamma ~\&~ \gamma=\delta\end{aligned} \therefore$ Option (1) satisfies the given condition

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Young’s modulus of elasticity $Y$ is expressed in terms of three derived quantities, namely, the gravitational constant $G$, Planck’s constant $h$ and the speed of light $c$, as $Y = {c}^{\alpha}{h}^{\beta}{G}^{\gamma}$. Which of the following is the correct option?
questions.solution:
Dimensions of Young's modulus: $\left[{M}^{1}{L}^{– 1}T{}^{– 2}\right]$

Dimensions of velocity of light: $\left[{M}^{0}{L}^{1}{T}^{– 1}\right]$

Dimensions of Planck's constant: $\left[{M}^{1}{L}^{2}{T}^{– 1}\right]$

Dimensions of Gravitational constant: $\left[{M}^{– 1}{L}^{3}{T}^{– 2}\right]$

Now, as given in the question$

$Y = {c}^{\alpha}{h}^{\beta}{G}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ $\left[{M}^{1}{L}^{– 1}T{}^{– 2}\right]$ = {$\left[{M}^{0}{L}^{1}{T}^{– 1}\right]$}^{\alpha}{$\left[{M}^{1}{L}^{2}{T}^{– 1}\right]$}^{\beta}{$\left[{M}^{– 1}{L}^{3}{T}^{– 2}\right]$}^{\gamma}$

Comparing exponent of the M, L & T both sides, we get$

$1 = \beta - \gamma ⇒ \beta = 1 + \gamma . . . \left(1\right)$

$- 1 = \alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma . . . \left(2\right)

and $- 2 = - \alpha - \beta - 2\gamma . . .$\left(3\right)$

From equation(1) and (2), we get$

$- 1 = \alpha + 2$\left(1 + \gamma\right) + 3\gamma ⇒ \alpha + 5\gamma = - 3 . . . \left(4\right)

From equation(1)$ and (3), we get

$- 2 = - \alpha - \left(1 + \gamma\right) - 2\gamma ⇒ \alpha + 3\gamma = 1 . . . \left(5\right)

From equation(4)$ and equation(5), we get

$\alpha = 7, \gamma = – 2$ and then $\beta = 1 + \gamma = - 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a particular system of units, a physical quantity can be expressed in terms of the electric charge $e$, electron mass ${m}_{e}$. Planck's constant $h$, and Coulomb's constant $k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}$, where ${ε}_{0}$ is the permittivity of vacuum. In terms of these physical constants, the dimension of the magnetic field is $\left[B\right] = {\left[e\right]}^{\alpha}{\left[{m}_{e}\right]}^{\beta}{\left[h\right]}^{\gamma}{\left[k\right]}^{\delta}$. The value of $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta$ is _______.
questions.solution:
Given here: $\left[B\right] = {\left[e\right]}^{\alpha}{\left[{m}_{e}\right]}^{\beta}{\left[h\right]}^{\gamma}{\left[k\right]}^{\delta}$

The dimensions of $\left[e\right] = \left[Current \times time\right] = \left[IT\right] and \left[{m}_{e}\right] = \left[M\right]$, Planck's constant $\left[h\right] = \dfrac{Energy}{Frequency} = \dfrac{\left[M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}\right]}{\left[{T}^{- 1}\right]} = \left[M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 1}\right]$ and $\left[k\right] = \dfrac{1}{\left[{ε}_{0}\right]$} = {$\left[{M}^{- 1}{L}^{- 3}{T}^{4}{I}^{2}\right]}^{- 1} = \left[M{L}^{3}{T}^{- 4}{I}^{- 2}\right]

Using Principle$ of $homogeneity,

\left[{M}^{1}{T}^{- 2}{I}^{- 1}\right] = {\left[IT\right]}^{\alpha}{\left[M\right]}^{\beta}{\left[M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 1}\right]}^{\gamma}{\left[M{L}^{3}{T}^{- 4}{I}^{- 2}\right]}^{\delta}$

Comparing both sides, we get

$\beta + \gamma + \delta = 1 . . . \left(i\right)

$2\gamma + 3\delta = 0 . . . $\left(ii\right)$

$\alpha - \gamma - 4\delta = - 2 . . . \left(iii\right)

$\alpha - 2\delta = - 1 . . . $\left(iv\right)$

On solving above four equations, we get

$\alpha = 3, \beta = - 4, \gamma = 3$ and $\delta = 2$

So, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A physical quantity $\overset{\to}{S}$ is defined as $\overset{\to}{S} = \dfrac{\left(\overset{\to}{E} \times \overset{\to}{B}\right)}{{\mu}_{0}}$. where $\overset{\to}{E}$ is electric field, $\overset{\to}{B}$ is magnetic field and ${\mu}_{0}$ is the permeability of free space. The dimensions of $\overset{\to}{S}$ are the same as the dimensions of which of the following quantity/quantities?
questions.solution:
Dimension of& $\dfrac{Force}{Length \times Time}= \dfrac{MLT- 2}{LT} = {MT}^{- 3}$

Dimensions of $\dfrac{Power}{Area} = \dfrac{Force \times Velocity}{Area} = \dfrac{{MLT}^{- 2} \times {LT}^{- 1}}{L2} = {MT}^{- 3}$,~

Dimension of Electric field& $\left(E\right), \left[E\right] = {MA}^{- 1}{LT}^{- 3}$

Dimensions of Magnetic field~$\left(B\right); \left[B\right] = {MA}^{- 1}T^{- 2}$

Dimension of magnetic permeability~$\left({μ}_{0}\right); \left[{μ}_{0}\right] = {MA}^{- 2}T^{- 2}L$

Therefore,~dimensions of& $S,\left[S\right] = \left[\dfrac{EB}{\mu0}\right] = \dfrac{\left({MA}^{- 1}{LT}^{- 3}\right)\left({MA}^{- 1}T^{- 2}\right)}{{MA}^{- 2}T^{- 2}L} = {MT}^{- 3}$
questions.question: A physical quantity $\overset{\to}{S}$ is defined as $\overset{\to}{S} = \dfrac{\left(\overset{\to}{E} \times \overset{\to}{B}\right)}{{\mu}_{0}}$. where $\overset{\to}{E}$ is electric field, $\overset{\to}{B}$ is magnetic field and ${\mu}_{0}$ is the permeability of free space. The dimensions of $\overset{\to}{S}$ are the same as the dimensions of which of the following quantity/quantities?
questions.explanation:
Dimension of $\dfrac{Force}{Length \times Time}= \dfrac{{MLT}^{- 2}}{LT} = {MT}^{- 3}$

Dimensions of $\dfrac{Power}{Area} = \dfrac{Force \times Velocity}{Area} = \dfrac{{MLT}^{- 2} \times {LT}^{- 1}}{{L}^{2}} = {MT}^{- 3}$,

Dimension of Electric field $\left(E\right), \left[E\right] = {MA}^{- 1}{LT}^{- 3}$

Dimensions of Magnetic field $\left(B\right); \left[B\right] = {MA}^{- 1}{T}^{- 2}$

Dimension of magnetic permeability $\left({\mu}_{0}\right); \left[{\mu}_{0}\right] = {MA}^{- 2}{T}^{- 2}L$

Therefore, dimensions of $S,\left[S\right] = \left[\dfrac{EB}{{\mu}_{0}}\right] = \dfrac{\left({MA}^{- 1}{LT}^{- 3}\right)\left({MA}^{- 1}{T}^{- 2}\right)}{{MA}^{- 2}{T}^{- 2}L} = {MT}^{- 3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sometimes it is convenient to construct a system of units so that all quantities can be expressed in terms of only one physical quantity. In one such system, dimensions of different quantities are given in terms of a quantity $X$ as follows: $\left[position\right] = \left[{X}^{\alpha}\right]; \left[speed\right] = \left[{X}^{\beta}\right]; \left[acceleration\right] = \left[{X}^{p}\right];\left[linearmomentum\right]$ = $\left[{X}^{q}\right]$; $\left[force\right]$ = $\left[{X}^{r}\right]$. Then
questions.solution:
$\left[\dfrac{momentum}{Force}\right] = {X}^{p - r}$

$⇒ \left[\dfrac{mv}{ma}\right] = {X}^{p - r}$

$⇒ \left[\dfrac{v}{a}\right] = {X}^{p - r}$

but given that $\dfrac{v}{a} = {X}^{\beta - p}$

So,

$p - r = \beta - p ⇒ 2p = \beta + r . . . \left(1\right)$

$\left[\dfrac{spee{d}^{2}}{acceleration}\right] = \left[position\right] ⇒ \dfrac{{X}^{2\beta}}{{X}^{p}} = {X}^{\alpha} ⇒ 2\beta - p = \alpha ⇒ p + \alpha = 2\beta . . . \left(2\right)$

and

$\left[\dfrac{force}{linearmomentum}\right] = \left[\dfrac{acceleration}{speed}\right] ⇒ \left[\dfrac{{X}^{r}}{{X}^{q}}\right] = \left[\dfrac{{X}^{p}}{{X}^{\beta}}\right] ⇒ r - q = p - \beta ⇒ p + q - r = \beta . . . \left(3\right)$

questions.solution:

\left[L\right]$ = $\left[Length\right]$

$= \left[{L}^{2}{L}^{- 4}\right]
$= $\left[{L}^{- 2}\right] ⇒ \left(D\right) is correct.

Linear momentum \left[P\right] = \left[ML{T}^{- 1}\right] = \left[L ⋅ {L}^{- 2}\right]

questions.q: Consider an expanding sphere of instantaneous radius $R$ whose total mass remains constant. The expansion is such that the instantaneous density $ρ$ remains uniform throughout the volume. The rate of fractional change in density $\left(\dfrac{1}{ρ}\dfrac{dρ}{dt}\right)$ is constant. The velocity $v$ of any point on the surface of the expanding sphere is proportional to
questions.solution:
Density of sphere is $ρ = \dfrac{m}{v} = \dfrac{3m}{4π{R}^{3}}$

$\to \dfrac{1}{ρ}\dfrac{dρ}{dt} = - \dfrac{3}{R}\dfrac{dR}{dt}$

Since $\to \dfrac{1}{ρ}\dfrac{dρ}{dt}$ is constant

$∴ \dfrac{dR}{dt} ∝ R$

questions.q: A length - scale $\left(l\right)$ depends on the permittivity $\left(ε\right)$ of a dielectric material, Boltzmann constant ${k}_{B}$ , the absolute temperature T, the number per unit volume (n) of certain charged particles, and the charge (q) carried by each of the particles, Which of the following expressions (s) for $l$ is (are) dimensionally correct?
questions.solution:
We know,
$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{E}_{0}}\dfrac{{q}^{2}}{{r}^{2}} ⇒ \dfrac{{q}^{2}}{{E}_{0}} = \left(F{r}^{2}\right)4\pi$
So, dimension
$\dfrac{{q}^{2}}{{E}_{0}} = dim ⁡ \left(F{r}^{2}\right) = ML{T}^{- 2} \times {L}^{2} = M{L}^{3}{T}^{- 2}$
Similarly; $E = \dfrac{3}{2}{K}_{B}T ⇒ dim ⁡ \left({K}_{B}T\right) = dim ⁡ \left(Energy\right) = M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}$
(i) $\sqrt{\dfrac{n{q}^{2}}{E{k}_{B}T}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{L}^{- 3} \times M{L}^{3}{T}^{- 2}}{M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}} = \dfrac{1}{L}}$
(ii) $\sqrt{\dfrac{\left(E\right) \times vol}{F{r}^{2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{ML{T}^{- 2} \times {L}^{3}}{ML{T}^{- 2} \times {L}^{2}}} = L$
(iii) $\sqrt{\dfrac{F{r}^{2}{\left(vol\right)}^{\dfrac{2}{3}}}{( Kℇ )}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{ML{T}^{- 2} \times {L}^{2} \times {L}^{2}}{M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}}} = \sqrt{{L}^{3}} = {L}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}$
(iv) $\sqrt{\dfrac{F{r}^{2}{\left(vol\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{Energy}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{ML{T}^{- 2}{L}^{2} \times L}{M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}}} = L$

[ $∴$ dimension n = dim $\left(\dfrac{1}{vol}\right) = {L}^{- 3}$ ]

questions.q: Planck' constant $h$ , speed of light $c$ and gravitational constant $G$ are used to form a unit of length $L$ and a unit of mass $M$ . Then the correct option(s) is (are)
questions.solution:
$\left[h\right] = \left[M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 1}\right]$
$\left[c\right] = \left[L{T}^{- 1}\right]$
$\left[G\right] = \left[{M}^{- 1}{L}^{3}{T}^{- 2}\right]$
For unit of length
Let $L ∝ {h}^{x}{c}^{y}{G}^{z}$
$⇒$ From principle of homogeneity
$\left[LHS\right] = \left[RHS\right]$
$⇒ \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{0}\right] = {\left[M{L}^{2}{T}^{- 1}\right]}^{x}{\left[L{T}^{- 1}\right]}^{y}{\left[{M}^{- 1}{L}^{3}{T}^{- 2}\right]}^{z}$
${M}^{0}L{T}^{0} = {M}^{x - z}{L}^{2x + y + 3z}{T}^{- x - y - 2z}$
Comparing we get
$x - z = 0$
$2x + y + 3z = 1$
$- x - y - 2z = 0$
Solving we get, $x = \dfrac{1}{2}, y = \dfrac{- 3}{2}, z = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$L = \sqrt{\dfrac{hG}{{c}^{3}}}$
For unit of mass
Let $M ∝ {h}^{x}{c}^{y}{G}^{z}$
Solving in similar manner as above
We get $x = \dfrac{1}{2}, y = \dfrac{1}{2}, z = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$
$M = \sqrt{\dfrac{hc}{G}}$

questions.q: Paragraph: A dense collection of equal number of electrons and positive ions is called neutral plasma. Certain solids containing fixed positive ions surrounded by free electrons can be treated as neutral plasma. Let $N$ be the number density of free electrons, each of mass $m$. When the electrons are subjected to an electric field, they are displaced relatively away from the heavy positive ions.If the electric field becomes zero, the electrons being to oscillate about the positive ions with a natural angular frequency $\omega_p$, which is called the plasma frequency. To sustain the oscillations, a time varying electric field needs to be applied that has an angular frequency $\omega$, where a part of the energy is absorbed and a part of it is reflected. As $\omega$ approaches $\omega_p$, all the free electrons are set to resonance together and all the energy is reflected. This is the explanation of high reflectivity of metals.Question: Taking the electronic charge as $e$ and the permittivity as $\varepsilon_0$, use dimensional analysis to determine the correct expression for $\omega_p$.
questions.solution:
$N=$ Number of electrons per unit volume

$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad[$ N] & =$\left[\mathrm{L}^{-3}\right],[$ e]=[q] \\
& =[I t]=[$\mathrm{AT}]$\\
{$\left[\varepsilon_0\right] } & =\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{ L}^{-3} \mathrm{ T}^4 \mathrm{ A}^2\right]
\end{aligned}

Substituting$ the $dimensions, we can see that,

\left.\sqrt{\frac{N e^2}{m \varepsilon_0}}\right]=\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]

Angular frequency has also the dimension \left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right].$\therefore$ Correct option is (c).
Analysis of Question
(i) From calculation point of view, question is moderately difficult. Otherwise it is simple.
(ii) Students may commit a mistake in the dimensions of $N. It is not dimensionless.
